extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, researchers, and rail/transport safety professionals
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia case-study article summarizing the Lac-Mégantic runaway train derailment (July 6, 2013), its causes, chronology, casualties, emergency response, regulatory findings, and subsequent regulatory/operational changes. Contains quoted rules, regulatory responses, investigation findings, and policy recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport Canada track-maintenance allowance (ties vs speed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transport Canada permits a railway to remain in service with as few as five solid ties and 14 damaged ties in a 12-metre (39 ft) section of track, provided trains are limited to 16 km/h (10 mph) on straight flat track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context in article: MMA deferred maintenance and track conditions deteriorated; regulators allowed continued operation under speed restrictions. Shows a regulatory trade-off: minimum tie condition tolerated if speed limits imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: CROR Section 112 — handbrake requirements for parked equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 112 of the Canadian Rail Operating Rules states 'when equipment is left at any point a sufficient number of hand brakes must be applied to prevent it from moving' and 'the effectiveness of the hand brakes must be tested'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains how an engineer tests handbrakes by seeing if the train budges when trying to push and pull with locomotive power; also notes disagreement about how many brakes are 'sufficient' and that Transport Canada did not give specific guidance on counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: TSB estimate of required handbrakes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Transportation Safety Board (TSB) estimated that somewhere between 17 and 26 hand brakes would have been needed to secure the MMA train involved in the Lac-Mégantic accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as investigatory guidance/estimate based on train length, grade, and likely application force; contrasts with MMA procedures and the engineer's reported number of handbrakes set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parking procedure and stabilization test (recommended practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Usual practice: when parking a train an engineer applies brakes on the cars by releasing air from the train line so air in car reservoirs applies the car brakes; a stabilization test (possible with a two-person crew) involves releasing all air brakes and ensuring the hand brakes alone hold the train.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that the engineer incorrectly left locomotive air brakes on, giving a false impression that hand brakes alone would hold the train, and that a two-person crew would have enabled a proper stabilization test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-brake system / locomotive compressor requirement and reset safety control wiring
rubrics_metrics.description: Air brakes are supplied by compressors on locomotives; when a locomotive is shut off the compressor no longer supplies the brake system and slow leakage can deplete pressure. The TSB found the 'reset safety control' on the lead locomotive was not wired to set the entire train's brakes in the event of an engine failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article notes that some locomotives can automatically restart the air-brake system if not shut down; wiring/design of safety controls that would set brakes on engine failure is highlighted as a safety shortcoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-Person Train Operation (SPTO) permitting and public input requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Freight trains operated by MMA were allowed SPTO (single-person train operation) status; the article notes the 'permit' process, which requires public input, was not followed in this case and regulators allowed manpower reduction after negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a governance/process criterion: reductions in crew size that affect safety should follow formal permit processes that include public input.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOT-111 tank car design concerns and replacement standard (TC-117)
rubrics_metrics.description: DOT-111 tank cars (CTC-111A in Canada) were described as having 'a high incidence of tank failures during accidents' and 'inadequate design'. Since 2011 Canada required thicker shells but older models remained allowed; after the accident DOT-111 cars were to be withdrawn from transporting crude oil by Nov 1, 2016 and a new tank car design, the TC-117, became the new standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites NTSB and industry concern; guidance implies that tank car design standards (thicker shells, newer TC-117 spec) are an essential safety requirement for transporting flammable liquids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track circuit installation to detect train presence
rubrics_metrics.description: The track at the relevant location was not equipped with track circuits to alert the rail traffic controller to the presence of a runaway train.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied safety criterion: install and maintain wayside/track circuits or other detection systems so controllers receive alerts of moving equipment on mains, especially in high-risk locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational restrictions imposed on MMA when service resumed
rubrics_metrics.description: When MMA was again allowed to operate between Sherbrooke and Lac-Mégantic (Dec 18, 2013), operations within Lac-Mégantic were subject to numerous restrictions: prohibition on transport of dangerous cargo; a train's manifest being released no less than four hours ahead; no parking on tracks within 4 km (2 mi) of the town centre; a conductor and engineer must be on board; and a train's speed must not exceed 16 km/h (10 mph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are concrete operational conditions imposed as safety mitigations after the accident; they illustrate regulatory levers (cargo bans, staffing, speed, advance notice) to reduce risk in populated areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability insurance adequacy and notification requirement to CTA
rubrics_metrics.description: The Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA) indicated carriers must 'notify the Agency in writing without delay if [...] the [...] operation has changed so that the liability insurance coverage may no longer be adequate.' The CTA suspended MMA's Certificate of Fitness because of failure to obtain adequate insurance coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a regulatory/administrative requirement tying operational fitness to adequate liability insurance and timely notification of material operational changes that affect insurance adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: FRA Emergency Order: attendance and securement requirements (U.S. response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the accident the U.S. Federal Railroad Administration issued an 'Emergency Order Establishing Additional Requirements for Attendance and Securement of Certain Freight Trains and Vehicles on Mainline Track or Mainline Siding Outside of a Yard or Terminal' (Aug 2, 2013).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes immediate federal enforcement requirements in the U.S. context for attendance and securement of trains carrying hazardous materials; cited as an example of regulatory emergency action post-incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crude oil content testing before shipment
rubrics_metrics.description: The article references later regulatory guidance that 'Crude oil must be tested before shipped by rail, U.S. regulators say.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied standard: shippers/operators should characterize and test the properties of crude oil before transport to identify volatility/flashpoint and adjust handling/packaging/controls accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routing and siting policy for hazardous-materials trains (avoid downtown cores)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article records calls and proposals to reroute the line to bypass Lac-Mégantic's downtown core and notes historical proposals to reroute were not implemented because of cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy/land-use criterion: routing hazardous-materials trains away from dense downtown/urban cores is presented as a risk mitigation approach; the article presents it as a recommended or proposed safety measure rather than an existing universal rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locomotive and equipment securement / cab locking expectation (practice vs rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: TSB found MMA's operating plan was to leave the train parked on the main line, unattended, with an unlocked locomotive cab, accessible to the public, and with no additional protection; the article also notes there were no rules against leaving a train unlocked, running and unattended even if it contained dangerous materials and was stopped on the main line on a slope in a residential area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights a gap between safe-practice expectations (lock and secure locomotives containing hazardous cargo) and the absence of an explicit regulatory requirement at the time; it functions as an implied criterion for securement policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency response tactics for burning tank cars
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency response actions documented include dousing unexploded cars with high-pressure water to prevent further explosions, bringing special fire-retardant foam from a refinery, creating firebreaks, and blocking manholes as burning oil spread into the storm sewer system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are tactical/operational response practices for incidents involving burning crude oil tank cars and urban fire spread; they serve as practical guidance for emergency planning and mutual-aid response.
